summary.text: Manganese nodules are lumps on the sea bottom made of layers of iron and manganese hydroxides built up around a core.
Their growth is one of the slowest known geological processes, about a centimetre over several million years, yet in places they cover more than 70% of the sea floor.
Because they are rich in nickel, copper, manganese and other rare metals, they have drawn growing interest as a mining resource.

facts.label: Typical size
facts.value: 3 to 10 cm, about the size of hen's eggs

facts.label: First discovered
facts.value: 1868, in the Kara Sea off Siberia

items.prompt: A nodule grows about a centimetre every several million years. If one is the size of a hen's egg, roughly how long has it been growing?

options.label: A few decades
A few centuries
A few thousand years
Millions of years

items.explain: Most nodules are 3 to 10 cm across, and at about a centimetre per several million years that takes millions of years.

items.prompt: Why are mining companies interested in collecting these lumps from the seabed?

options.label: They are full of nickel, copper and other metals
They hold pockets of oil and natural gas
They are valuable gemstones once polished
They release fresh drinking water when melted

items.explain: The high relative abundance of nickel, copper, manganese and other rare metals has increased interest in nodules as a mining resource.

items.prompt: You lift a nodule whose lower half was buried in seabed mud. How does its underside usually compare with its top?

options.label: Smoother, polished by the mud
Rougher, from a different growth
Exactly the same as the top
Hollow, with the core worn out

items.explain: The buried bottom surface is generally rougher than the top because it grows in a different way.

items.prompt: A nodule from the deep sea is compared with one dug out of soil on land. What difference would you expect?

options.label: The land one contains no iron at all
The sea one is made of pure copper
The sea one has more manganese per iron
The two are always chemically identical

items.explain: Land nodules are usually richer in iron, while marine nodules tend to have higher manganese-to-iron ratios.

items.prompt: These nodules turn up in the shallow Baltic Sea, the deep central Pacific and even in lakes. What does that tell you?

options.label: They form only beside active volcanoes
They form only in fresh water
They form only in very deep water
They form in both shallow and deep water

items.explain: Polymetallic nodules are found in both shallow and deeper waters, and even in lakes.

items.prompt: If you sliced a nodule in half, what would the inside look like?

options.label: Rings of metal oxides around a core
A single solid lump of pure metal
An empty space filled with trapped gas
Loose sand held in by a thin shell

items.explain: Nodules are made of concentric layers of iron and manganese hydroxides or oxides built up around a core.
